selected.title: AI’s progress on theoretical problems is accelerating across sciences
selected.summary: A study discussed by WIRED reports that top AI models’ success on selected theoretical problems across several fields rose from about 2% in mid-2024 to about 35% in mid-2026. This measures performance on a set of problems, not general scientific ability or independent discovery.
selected.why_it_matters: If AI tools become more capable across disciplines, research workflows, training and the role of human verification may all change.
selected.challenge_question: What change did a study report in AI performance on selected theory problems?
selected.answer_explanation: The reported benchmark comparison found performance rising from roughly 2% in mid-2024 to roughly 35% in mid-2026 on the problems studied; it should not be generalized to all scientific tasks.
selected.butterfly_question: If AI can solve more technical problems, which parts of scientific work should remain distinctly human?

selected.title: Chinese pottery points to Great Zimbabwe’s far-reaching trade
selected.summary: A report on archaeological work at Great Zimbabwe describes Chinese pottery fragments at the medieval African city, adding evidence of connections spanning long distances. The find offers a vivid way to explore trade networks and the sophistication of precolonial African societies.
selected.why_it_matters: Material evidence of long-distance exchange can reshape how people understand medieval African economies and global connections.
selected.challenge_question: What do Chinese pottery fragments at Great Zimbabwe suggest?
selected.answer_explanation: The reported pottery find supports the interpretation that Great Zimbabwe had far-reaching trade connections. The fragments alone do not establish the exact route or nature of contact.
selected.butterfly_question: What can a traded object reveal about the people and networks that connected distant societies?

Chinese Pottery Reveals Great Zimbabwe’s Global Trade Network

selected.title: Webb may have caught a distant supernova just days after its explosion
selected.summary: Researchers reported a possible supernova in a galaxy seen as it was about 1.2 billion years after the Big Bang. Observations suggest it may have been detected only days after the explosion, but the event and its interpretation remain under study.
selected.why_it_matters: Catching a distant stellar explosion early could help scientists investigate how massive stars lived and died in the young universe.
selected.challenge_question: What makes Webb’s possible distant supernova observation unusual?
selected.answer_explanation: The reporting says observations may have captured the transient roughly four to ten days after explosion. It is a candidate event, not a confirmed supernova classification.
selected.butterfly_question: How could observing a star’s final days help explain the ingredients and evolution of early galaxies?

sources.title: Webb spots possible early-universe supernova just days after it happened

selected.title: A famous impact crater may be far younger than scientists thought
selected.summary: New dating places an American impact crater roughly 100 million years younger than previous estimates, near a major Late Devonian extinction event. The timing raises a possible connection, but does not show that the impact caused the extinction.
selected.why_it_matters: Revised dates can change how scientists investigate links between extraterrestrial impacts and major changes in life on Earth.
selected.challenge_question: What does the crater’s revised age suggest about its timing?
selected.answer_explanation: The revised dating places the impact near the Late Devonian extinction event. Temporal proximity raises a hypothesis; it does not establish that the impact caused the extinction.
selected.butterfly_question: When an impact and an extinction line up in time, what evidence is needed to show one affected the other?

selected.title: A large asteroid appears to spin once in just over four minutes
selected.summary: A report on Vera C. Rubin Observatory data describes an asteroid about 2.5 kilometers across rotating in a little over four minutes, making it an unusually large ultra-fast rotator. The discovery also illustrates how new survey methods can revise measurements from telescope observations.
selected.why_it_matters: Asteroid spin can reveal clues about internal strength and structure, while better surveys improve our picture of small bodies in the solar system.
selected.challenge_question: About how long does the reported large asteroid take to rotate once?
selected.answer_explanation: The report describes a roughly 2.5-kilometer asteroid completing a rotation in just over four minutes. The result depends on the study’s revised analysis of observations.
selected.butterfly_question: What can an asteroid’s spin tell us about the forces holding a rocky world together?
